extracted.intended_audience: early 18th-century literate coffee‑house readers, theatre‑goers, and genteel critics
extracted.subtask_description: Short satirical and critical periodical essays (coffee‑house journalism) offering judgments on theatre, poetry, taste, patronage, and social character. The rubric concerns how such pieces should observe, exemplify, and judge manners, style, and literary works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theatrical characters to reveal an age's taste
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of knowing the taste of an age so good as by the observations of the persons represented in their comedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics should read plays as social documents: the kinds of characters dramatists include (e.g., Shakespeare's women vs. modern actresses) indicate the freedoms, manners, and dominant virtues of the period. Examples: Shakespeare's women reflect a time when women had less freedom in conversation; modern comedies show coquettes, wit, and political female figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray women according to social reality of their time
rubrics_metrics.description: Women in older dramas are typically mothers, sisters, daughters, and wives rather than shining wits or disputants; a playwright should draw female characters as they are in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anachronistic imaginings of women's roles; the absence or presence of coquettes, virtuosas, and political women onstage signals social change. When creating or judging female characters, consider whether they plausibly reflect contemporary freedoms and conversational roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of virtue should show inward genuineness
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly virtuous character (exemplified by 'Aspasia') manifests humility, simplicity, economy, and steady piety without seeking praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good characters embody virtues as part of their inner disposition: 'the most exact economist, without appearing busy; the most strictly virtuous, without tasting the praise of it; and shuns applause with as much industry, as others do reproach.' Readers should be able to 'fix' the character on one person because of distinct, consistent traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid characters whose virtue is performative or envious
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti‑pattern exemplified by 'Poluglossa' — a character whose innocence is merely a restraint with envy, who speaks endlessly of others' vices without possessing genuine virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should flag characters whose moralizing is hypocrisy or social posturing. Such figures are characterized by continual discourse of vice and a susceptibility to praise rather than genuine moral feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedications and panegyrics should avoid obvious flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Panegyrics frequently border on flattery; a writer should beware of raising 'a number of plants' in praise that will be mistaken for flattery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing dedications or praises to patrons, keep justice and plainness to avoid being mistaken for flattery. The essay lampoons transactional patronage (dedications as purchase) and implies that genuine compliment should not read as mercenary praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical and scientific prose should be lively in matter and language
rubrics_metrics.description: To remedy the imputation of dryness and dullness, write philosophy in a more lively method, both as to the matter and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fable, vivacious hypotheses, and accessible imagery (e.g., a playful cosmological fable) to make learned subjects engaging to a coffee‑house audience; appendices or humorous apologias can defend oddities in style.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Sublime: prefer natural, context‑appropriate similes
rubrics_metrics.description: The true greatness of soul is best represented by natural, appropriate similes arising from the speaker's imagination, rather than forced metaphors in tragedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived similes when describing great sorrow or heroic action ('nothing so forced and constrained as what we frequently meet with in tragedies'). Favor images that fit the person and time; prefer sublime, elevated images (e.g., ministering angel) that elevate the hero without honoring the brute. Example of good practice: lines from 'The Campaign' showing an angelic simile that both praises a general and fits contemporary feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic simile as a relief for intense thought
rubrics_metrics.description: It is natural and proper for a poet, struck with a great image, to relieve himself from the burden of thought by uttering simile and metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow and value similes that emerge organically from a speaker's meditative state ('to relieve and clear himself from the burthen of thought'); they can be the highest act of poetic expression when occasioned by the mind's working.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic poetry should balance chronicle and the heroic style
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic performance should be both chronicle and poem, keeping the ordinary ideas of a march while remaining familiar and yet heroic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic or martial poems should preserve national memory and praise heroes without losing readability or natural sentiment; they should make the particular actions memorable when prose monuments fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical and public representations should be managed fairly and decently
rubrics_metrics.description: Public sales/auctions and theatrical exhibitions ought to be conducted honestly; clandestine deals and indecent or abusive entertainments (e.g., puppets insulting public figures) are censurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should call out unfair management (missing lots, secret purchasers) and condemn lewd or disrespectful theatrical practices that damage public trust or abuse reputations. Example anti‑pattern: puppet‑show personating and speaking saucily of real persons.
